compiled_state.description:
## Summary

`doctor` now scans the OPERATOR'S HOME for MCP client configs (`~/.codex/config.toml`,
`~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`, `~/.claude.json`). Any test that invokes `doctor_cli` therefore
reads live machine state it does not control, which makes those tests non-hermetic. Three were
observed failing and then passing across repeat runs on an unchanged tree.

## Almost certainly my own doing — recorded so nobody hunts a ghost

I introduced the HOME scan (change 2272, `doctor_mcp_client.py`). While another session's test
tier was running, I was CONCURRENTLY REWRITING those exact files for the Layer 1 credential
migration: `~/.claude.json` and `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` rewritten via `json.dumps`,
`~/.codex/config.toml` edited twice, `~/.zshrc` appended.

A `json.dumps` rewrite is not atomic — there is a window where the file is truncated or partial.
A concurrent `doctor` read landing in that window gets a parse error rather than the config, and
takes a different code path. That fits the observed signature exactly: intermittent, unreproducible
on a quiet machine, and correlated with nothing in the tree.

The other agent initially reported these as deterministic and host-coupled, then corrected itself
to intermittent after three clean repeat runs, and declined to retry them away. Both calls were
right.

## Why it is still a real defect, not just my interference

Even with nobody editing anything, these tests depend on whatever client configs happen to exist
on the machine running them. That means:

- they pass or fail based on developer-local state that is not in the repo;
- a developer with a broken personal Codex config sees failures unrelated to their change;
- CI passes only because runners have no such configs — i.e. the coupling is invisible where it
  would be caught.

I deliberately made the client findings ADVISORY (excluded from `doctor`'s exit code) for exactly
this reason, and added `--strict-mcp-clients` as the opt-in. That prevents the findings from
FAILING a store-health gate, but it does not make the tests hermetic — the scan still runs, still
reads HOME, and can still misbehave on malformed input.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `doctor` tests are hermetic: they inject a `home` (the scanner already takes one) or set
      `HOME` to a fixture directory, so no test reads the real operator's configs.
- [ ] A malformed or partially-written client config degrades to a clear finding and cannot
      change `doctor`'s exit code or raise — concurrent-write safety, not just parse safety.
- [ ] The three affected tests (`test_doctor_dirty_tree` ×2, `test_doctor_mapping`) pass
      deterministically with an arbitrary HOME state.

## Note on the atomic-write half

If the concurrent-rewrite theory is right, the durable lesson is about the WRITER, not only the
reader: rewriting a config with `json.dumps` straight over the original leaves a window where any
concurrent reader sees a truncated file. Write to a temp file and `os.replace` it. That applies to
any tooling this project ships that edits user config in place.
compiled_state.title: doctor tests are non-hermetic: they read the operator's real HOME configs, so they flake when those change
